rewrites.5EF291F2: The marker was the model's assumption, not a measured cap. At the international routes' 76.0% load factor, 1.8 million inbound seats would carry about 1.37 million arrivals, fewer than the 1.57 million ACSA recorded in FY25/26. The model gives no seat table, load factors or frequencies behind the figure (Appendix A2). What binds in practice is the runway at peak hours in summer, at about 30 movements an hour, and no source yet gives peak-hour or seasonal slot headroom.[^134]
rewrites.63B4A348: Yet no seat flies direct to Asia: the network has no direct capacity to any Asian market. Thirteen of the 27 routes in the load table serve African or Indian Ocean points, and none serves Asia. A direct Asian route is a long-term prize, and the near-term seats sit with the hub carriers. The hub routes are not full. Dubai ran at 72.3%, Addis Ababa at 71.9% and Doha at 65.2% in the year to November 2025. On those routes marketing can still fill seats, which it cannot do on the eleven full ones.[^146]
rewrites.7FADE1BD: Connecting traffic is especially critical in the green season, which ties the winter schedule to the hub carriers' own priorities. New seats must therefore be won route by route and season by season, as New Zealand did with route-tied marketing (section 2.2).[^148]
rewrites.547B02F6: Cape Winelands Airport stays a scenario, not committed capacity. It is a private development at the old Fisantekraal airfield, some 30 km north of the city, with a first phase of about R8 billion. Its 3.5 km runway could take long-haul aircraft, its terminal is designed for 5.2 million passengers a year and it targets first passengers in 2028. Environmental appeals were dismissed in May 2026, but financial close, aviation licensing and airline commitments are not yet evidenced. Capacity and certainty pull apart: the certain fix comes last, and the earliest large option is the least certain.[^152]
rewrites.6BA7AA83: Berth space is not the limit. The single equipped berth can take 150 or more calls a season. Its limits are a 300m ship length, the South-Easter wind and the lack of shore power. The demand base is volatile. International passengers rose from 55,495 in 2022/23 to 100,255 in 2024/25, about 81% more; the 2025/26 split is not in hand. Reroutes made 20 of the 67 calls in 2023/24, and Red Sea diversions reverse when shipping normalises. The Diagnostic also rates the Port of Cape Town a binding constraint, with congestion and equipment failures affecting export and cruise reliability. Growth is set by the regional circuit that brings a ship for a season and by shore capacity on call days.[^155]
rewrites.75F7C769: The alternatives have room but are not yet ready to take the overflow. Township attractions are underused and overflow reserves under-marketed, yet CapeNature's reserves already draw more visitors: over the festive season Robberg's day visitors rose 50% and Stony Point's visitors 28%. Stony Point, the Overberg's penguin colony, is this report's alternative to Boulders. CapeNature is cautious about scaling international demand, because service readiness is uneven across its sites and most reserves lie two to three hours from the airport by road. Eleven of the 16 organisations see the offer as concentrated around Cape Town and a few icons. The peak must spread to product with room, under the capacity discipline New Zealand applies (section 2.2).[^162]
rewrites.20E4F785: Tourism weighs most in the smaller district economies. In 2023 tourist spend equalled 16.8% of GDPR on the West Coast and 15.6% in the Overberg. It equalled 7.0% in the Cape Winelands and 6.7% in the Metro. The district reviews give the same series for the Garden Route and the Central Karoo, 16.1% for each in 2023, which the Provincial Treasury has still to confirm. The Metro holds the volume, but a fall in visitors costs the outer districts more of their economy.[^166]
rewrites.1BDC0829: The Cape Winelands is the province's premium food and wine district and the nearest dispersal region to Cape Town. About 1.5 million visitors a year go to its participating attractions, on Wesgro's 2025 estimate. Visitor numbers fell while bed-nights rose by 20.2% for domestic and 37.5% for international visitors, over a period the source does not state. Wine estates dominate its 2,298 attraction records, and the Stellenbosch, Franschhoek and Paarl corridor holds most of the attractions, beds and restaurants. Mid-market accommodation is effectively absent outside Stellenbosch, and a product mix skewed to luxury excludes mid-market and family segments. Supply also tightens without warning in harvest, in wedding weeks and in the winter off-season.[^172]
rewrites.724FB71B: Access rests on one road. The N1 is the only reliable corridor, and the district has no scheduled air service, no tourism shuttle and no public transport. Beyond the N1, fuel, retail, healthcare and connectivity thin out, summer heat shortens the visiting season and truck congestion threatens the transit trade that sustains operators. Tourism offices are under-resourced and destination marketing is close to nil. The Infrastructure Report gives no pipeline for the district: its only slide in that position covers Route 62 and the Klein Karoo. No committed project can therefore be named for the Central Karoo itself.[^179]
rewrites.7F79097C: Six touring routes carry visitors between those districts, and one is rated ready for international visitors (Table 2.17). The Infrastructure Report rates each Ready, Developing or Gap on access, accommodation, safety and bookability. The Garden Route carries the same four ratings as the Cape Peninsula yet is rated Developing.[^180]
rewrites.1D1A9C44: The two routes nearest the city need management more than new product. On the Cape Peninsula, growth depends on visitor flow and resilience, because road access congests between the major attractions. The Cape Winelands route works as a short extension of a Cape Town stay. It functions as a set of separate destinations, since estates market themselves singly and sober transfers between them remain unsolved.[^181]
rewrites.343B1C2E: Online booking is one part of the sixth barrier to conversion, difficulty finding information (section 2.1), and the evidence does not show it to be the main limit on regional growth. Where rooms are listed, the next gain is quality that shows on the booking platforms, as in Valencia (section 2.2).
rewrites.136DDA3F: For the supply side the implication is twofold. First, short-term rentals supply much of the self-catering stock visitors already favour (section 2.3), so they belong in any count of regional beds. Second, letting concentrated in a few central wards adds to resident pressure, which the plan's spread in time and place is meant to ease.
rewrites.38691863: Stakeholders rate supply constraints the most severe of the three goals. Of the 223 rated insights from 16 organisations, 68 are filed under the supply goal: 44 rated High, 24 Medium and none Low, against 23 High of 64 on demand. Fourteen of the 16 organisations raised at least one. Internal mobility and route and product development drew 18 insights each, with 10 and 11 rated High (Table A.24). The ratings carry no stated definition and attach to these detailed rows; the 16 summarised supply insights carry none.[^200]
rewrites.7123CABC: Ships come for the circuit, not for one port. A line deploys a ship for a season when a full itinerary works, and Wesgro's prospectus sells Cape Town as the homeport for two. The east coast itinerary calls at Mossel Bay and Hermanus, then at Gqeberha, East London, Durban and Richards Bay. It runs on to Mozambique, the East African coast and the Indian Ocean islands. The west coast itinerary runs through Saldanha Bay and Port Nolloth to Namibia, Angola and St Helena.

inserts.text: The province holds one equipped port in that circuit. Mossel Bay handled 21 calls and about 13,000 passengers and opened a R22 million passenger facility in November 2025, yet ships anchor and tender there and only small and mid-sized ships call. Saldanha Bay has had 3 trial calls into an ore terminal, with no cruise berth or passenger facility. Calls rise when the circuit works, not when Cape Town markets harder.

Mossel Bay's own count differs: calls rose from four before COVID-19 to 27 a season. The Cruise Economic Contribution Study counts 21 passenger-day visits there in 2024/25, with 31,146 passengers and R46.3 million of spending. For 2025/26 Wesgro counts 13 cruise liner visits across Mossel Bay, Hermanus and Saldanha Bay together, with just over 7,150 passengers and R11.2 million of spending. The counts follow different definitions and are not reconciled.[^156]
